Mr. Beganovic, in your testimony here and in the Tadic case, the -- from those testimony, there is -- there is an impression that you have certain feelings about certain people in general, about the whole of people in general. It is not very nice to hear expressions such as the "Serb garbage" and the "Serb scum" and I sincerely hope that you do not think that.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Well, I don't really think that, but at the moment, it was a reflection of my psychological state. I now travel to Prijedor. I'm seeing Serb people as well. I have drink with them, but I did have also some conflicts, that is true, but I had conflicts with people who are criminals. And I went to Prijedor two months ago and I would walk around the town, having drinks with Serb people in Prijedor, and I don't have any problems with that in that regard whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I can conclude that as regards the two of us, we will say hello to each other when we meet on the street, and that we could have a drink together.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: There will be no problem about that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, does it mean that you have changed your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I haven't. However, unfortunately, I do have an objection here. An objection to one of the questions that was put by my learned colleague, Mr. Fila. He asked the question about visitors of Omarska and he mentioned the name of Zigic. Let me just remind him that his client, Radic, has already stated that he had never seen Zigic, and I think that the reference to Zigic in this case would be somehow inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. Ms. Hollis. You have the floor for the redirect. Re-examined by Ms. Hollis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Beganovic, during your questioning by Mr. Simic on behalf of accused Kvocka, you made a statement about a man you called Kuruzovic organising the TO. Who is Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Slobodan Kuruzovic was first of all my teacher and foremaster, and he taught mathematics. When I grew up, we became friends, and we often went to the area of Kozarac. We would spend weekends in the mountain hut over there, mountain lodge. But when the war broke out, he joined the Serb army. He was the first one to enter the front line in Croatia. He was one of the commanders. He came back from Croatia with a booty, that is common knowledge. He came back with a Mercedes on one occasion and with horses as well. He was one of the key men in Prijedor as regards the issues relating to the military and the SDS party. He was one of the best known people in Prijedor at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, that is sufficient for my question. When you say that "he was organising the TO", what do you mean by this term "TO"?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Well, the territorial defence. But the territorial defence of the Serb people, the Serb military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Kuruzovic, what is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: He is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During questioning about these weapons that you received from your father, you indicated that you received a hunting weapon with a sniper was the way it was translated. What is a sniper?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: A sniper is used for carbine rifles. You install it on a rifle so that you can also hunt at night. It was a custom at that time, it was a custom to carry that equipment when you went hunting for deer, wolves, boar and this type of game.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you talking about some type of scope for the rifle?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've been asked questions and you have agreed that on several occasions, you were convicted of various offences. Regarding the convictions in Prijedor involving pickpocketing and concealing stolen goods. When were those convictions, if you remember? What years?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: In early 1970s. I don't want to spend too much time on that. Those offences were actually extorted the same way extortions were made in Omarska. They were made by Mr. Miskovic who was dealing with juvenile delinquents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could cut you off on that. In the early 1970s, what would have been your age at that time? How old were you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And regarding the pickpocketing on the tram in Zagreb, how old were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: I think I was 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And regarding this traffic offences, drunk driving in Banja Luka, how old were you then?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: 25, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what exactly, to your knowledge, were you charged with in Novi Sad? What misconduct were you charged with?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: The man who was driving my car in Novi Sad went on an errand in Novi Sad. I remained in the cafe. There were five of us. We had come to Novi Sad on business. This man was a Serb, a young man who was my friend from Prijedor. His name was Brane Copija. So who -- he was at the wheel of the car, and he caused a minor traffic accident. The police arrived. I was not present. They made a report, and the policeman came later on to take the details of my insurance, because it was not in the car. So he came to me together with him. So I gave him my insurance number and I told him that the vehicle was insured. The person who was at the wheel was actually not guilty of that traffic accident, it was the woman who caused the accident. And a report was made thereof and this person had a coffee with us. He took all the details regarding the insurance, and I asked him that he should send the report to me as soon as possible and to send all the information to the insurance company branch in Prijedor. A month later, a report, a criminal report was made against me alleging that I had given him -- that I had bribed him with 100 German marks so that the report would be in my favour. And I didn't need that because I was not guilty. I was not at the wheel and I -- my vehicle was insured. I didn't have an opportunity -- I didn't even have an opportunity to bribe the policeman because I was not alone with him. And the policeman was supposed to be discharged, but they fabricated some evidence against me and they turned me into a criminal just as they had been doing since I was 15. And in the end --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could interrupt, that is sufficient for my purposes, thank you. Now, you also testified that approximately two months ago, you were in Prijedor and there was a verbal and physical incident there. What happened?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Well, as I said a moment ago, I visited a couple of friends, Serbs, from before the war who are also caterers. I visited a number of catering establishments. We were sitting, talking, having fun, just as we had before the war. And then I entered one of these bars and we started an argument in connection with Dusko Tadic's trial. How could I have said that he was there? He was never in Omarska. There was an argument. And then one friend of mine and I headed towards Sanski Most, and then we crossed the Sana River at Tukovi -- this is a neighbourhood -- we were met by Dusko Vujakovic [phoen]. He stopped us in front of the car. We came out of the car and there was a light physical showdown. That's all that happened. And now I hear that I have been charged in Prijedor, and that criminal proceedings have been instituted against me. So it only means that what happened before the war and during the war is still going on now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your direct testimony, you testified about events that occurred on the 30th of May, the day that you were taken to the camp. In your prior testimony, you indicated that you slept in late because you had had too much to drink the night before and that at some point you were awakened by your friend, Asif?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you testified that you began to listen to the radio and you heard these announcements about what to do. So when you were listening to the radio, hearing these announcements; do you recall what time of the day that was?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to object. My learned friend is referring back to his direct testimony and asking questions about his direct testimony. In my submission, re-examination is limited to areas of cross-examination which are left unclear. In my submission, my friend is trying to go further in -- with his direct testimony and that's line 18 of page 58. She's referring to his direct testimony. I don't think that's appropriate re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan, perhaps it is a bit too early to intervene because you remember very well that Mr. Simic spoke at length about this question of radio reports. So maybe we should wait for Ms. Hollis to put her question.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: She has put her question to the witness and there's no reference to any cross-examination. That question comes on page 59, lines one through four. There's no reference to cross-examination in her question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan, until now, I thought that Ms. Hollis was making an introduction before putting her question. In any event, let me not interpret Madam Hollis. Let me give her the floor. Perhaps she has a response to the objection of Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, and perhaps when we have these discussions, it would be better for everyone if the witness would be asked to take their headphones off so there's no suggestion that they are influenced by the exchange. So I would ask the witness be asked to take the headphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please take off your headphones. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These questions were directed at the -- at trying to clarify the cross-examination regarding when the radio was listened to. In that regard, the Prosecution believes that it is possible to refer back to direct testimony and then in order to clarify, the witness has already said on direct it was the 30th of May that he was listening to the radio. On cross-examination, there was questions about whether he heard something during the night or early morning. I'm attempting to go clarify with the witness at what time of the day he listened to the radio. In his direct testimony, he indicated it was on the 30th. I'm simply trying to go back and clarify that. I can, if Your Honours wish it, technically point out the inconsistency in his cross and then go back to my other questions. I did not do that for expediency, but I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand now. Mr. O'Sullivan, you still abide by your objection after this clarification by Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have no objection if re-examination is limited to matters raised in cross-examination which are unclear, and I didn't see that happening, Your Honour, and that was the basis of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So the objection is overruled. Madam Hollis, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If the witness would put the headphones back on, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your testimony, when you were testifying about listening to announcements being made on the radio, what time of the day or night was it that you were listening to these announcements?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: It was during the daytime, about 11.00 or 12.00, I don't know, up to 1.00, at Dr. Esad Sadikovic's house. Then I fled from that soldier who fired at me, and then I entered the other house and there we listened too, so that must have been about 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon. We listened to the radio all day and they were broadcasting announcements, until they arrested as many men as they needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, to be clear, what date is it that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: The 30th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked several questions about the man you knew as Krkan, that as his nickname, the man --

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- you saw in Omarska camp. A few of those questions were posed that you had indicated in your testimony that you saw him pass by the restaurant a few times, and then you were asked if you saw him occasionally. Now, I'd like to ask you a few questions to clarify how often you saw Krkan in the camp. First of all, when you were on the pista, how frequently would you see Krkan?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Probably every time he was on duty in his shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can estimate for the Court, how frequently would that be? How often would you have seen him?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Well, that would probably be every other day, roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On every other day, roughly, that you would see him, how many times during the day would you see him?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Sometimes I might have seen him ten times; other times, twice. It depends how often we were told to bend our heads down to face the concrete. Sometimes we spent all day on our stomachs, up to 12 hours. Sometimes they let us sit normally for a couple of hours and then to lie down again, and so it went on. So if we were in a sitting position, we could see him more or less non-stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were on the pista, where was it? You have testified on cross-examination that you saw him near the restaurant building. Were there any other areas that you saw him while you were on the pista?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to object. This is examination-in-chief. I have cross-examined after the questions put by the Prosecution. Now we are expanding again. I think the Prosecutor has gone beyond the scope of the cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The questions were placed to the witness about when he saw Mr. Krkan, and when the questions were posed, some numeric qualifying word was used, "occasionally", "a few times." I tried to clarify that. Also he was asked, "You saw him near the restaurant building." I'm trying to clarify, again, where. So the question of locations was again put in question by the cross-examination. I'm simply trying to clarify where he was seen, if he was seen in locations other than near the restaurant building. That was raised on cross-examination. I believe it is a legitimate area of inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I think that the witness got up to point to the exact place. In any event, let us hear what Mr. Fila has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked him how many times he saw him, in what period of time, and the Prosecutor has clarified that point and I agree with that. But the places where he said he saw Krkan were indicated in response to the question of the Prosecutor, and I actually had asked him to point them out with the pointer. Anything beyond that is fresh direct. Because the Prosecutor asked, "Where else did you see him?" That's a new question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis, can you rephrase, or refer to the question from the cross-examination and then make your clarification. If it is repetitious, please don't do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Beganovic, during cross-examination you were asked if you saw the accused Krkan on a few occasions in Omarska. At one point you were also asked if you saw him a few times. Then you were asked if you saw him near the restaurant building. You were specifically asked by Defence counsel at one point to point out the "glass house" where you said you had seen him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: At least that is what was interpreted to me, Your Honours. We can check the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You pointed to a certain area. Now, you indicated you saw him at that certain area of the restaurant in response to that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my questions are simply: Did he see him in any other areas, because it was in response to a specific location that he got up and pointed. That's my review of the transcript, as I saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, excuse me, but we are not going to insist on this question further. It's an important question. If the Prosecutor can't ask that question, the Judges would ask that question. It is an important question for justice.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So put your question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Beganovic, in addition to that area you pointed out near the restaurant where you saw Krkan, what other areas, if any, in the camp did you see Mr. Krkan?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: I saw him later on, as I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Witness. Can you get up and point out the places, please.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: He would sometimes come out of this room [indicates], which is known as Mujo's room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. If Mr. Fila wants to, he can go up to the model, please. Can you see well? I'm sorry for interrupting, Witness. Ms. Hollis, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you indicated that he would sometimes come out of Mujo's room, and you were pointing to the side of the restaurant building that is away from the Judges; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: And we would be lined up here to sit there. They would let us get some fresh air, so this would happen sometimes. So that when we came out of Mujo's room, we could see all the guards going by, we could see them. Sometimes we could smoke, if we had cigarettes. So they were always walking around there. I don't know what they were doing. In any event, we could all see them. That's nothing strange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Beganovic, excuse me, but we're speaking of Krkan. You indicated that you would sometimes see him coming out of Mujo's room. Who was coming out of Mujo's room?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: We, we, the inmates, the detainees were coming out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you would see him, where would he be when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: He would be walking around here [indicates], near the pista. He would go into the restaurant, come back. They would walk around here [indicates], around us. How do I know what they were doing? Anyway, they were walking around here [indicates] on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis, I'm sorry for interrupting you. Could the usher keep the camera focused. Could the witness point one end and the other end of the movements, instead of using the pointer left and right. Will you tell us, from one end to the other end, please. Madam Hollis, can you help us?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have indicated a broad area where you would see Krkan walking about. Could you use the pointer and show the parameters of that area, if you will. So point first to the area that would be closest to you when you came out of Mujo's room, where you saw him, and then point to the area you saw him that would be farthest away. If you could help us with that.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: The whole of this area [indicates], a metre or two away from me, if we were sitting here [indicates]. There's only a couple of metres to this semicircle. Then the kombi van would be here and he would pass by us. So there was no distance between us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's focus on when you saw him and when you were on the pista. Could you indicate what areas of the pista you saw him? And if you saw him all about the pista, if you would simply say that.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: No. I would only see him when he came out of this entrance here [indicates]. He would either go this way or that way. But we weren't really interested in watching, all we cared about was that we wouldn't be called out and that the guards wouldn't mistreat us. Whether he was going left or right didn't concern us much. It's only a couple of metres away from us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Beganovic, then, you have indicated with your pointer that there were times when you would see Krkan coming out of the entrance, the main entrance of the restaurant building, and you would see him either going to areas to the left or going to areas to the right. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what other areas around the camp, and could you point to them one by one, what others did you see Krkan during your time in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: He would spend some time here [indicates]. While we were sitting there, we would say, "There's Krkan up there," and we were watching to see whether he would go up or come down, because we were afraid of every guard coming out of this door [indicates], whether they would start beating or what --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me a moment.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: We could see through the glass whether it was Krkan or Kvocka or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Beganovic, excuse me for interrupting you. You have pointed to something and you said you would see him there. Now, would you point to that again and tell us what that is, please? You pointed to that circular structure.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Point to that again, please.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that? Is that a window that you're pointing to?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes. It's a large glass surface, semicircular surface. And from the pista, one could clearly see who was coming down the steps, who was dwindling there, who was standing there. One could see it clearly. The face of the person could be identified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there any other areas in the camp that you yourself saw Krkan during your time in the camp? If there are, would you please point to those areas.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Other areas, except for this glass partition in the area in front of the restaurant, I didn't see him in any other place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you could leave the -- if the witness could leave off the earphones, please. Your Honours, the Prosecution believes that, except for accused Zigic, about whom there was no cross-examination, that identification has been brought into issue on cross-examination as to all of the other accused. We ask the Chamber what procedure, if any, will be allowed for in-court identifications?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Madam Hollis, but I didn't quite understand. That must be my fault. Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'm sure it's me, Your Honour. During the course of cross-examination, questions were asked that, in the Prosecution's view, calls the identity of the individuals named by the witness into question. So our question is: What procedure do you wish to follow for in-court identification of accused, or will you allow such procedure at all? In other words, now at this point in time, for the witness, if possible, to identify the accused of whom he has spoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis, I know that you put a question to us, but we would like to ask you, what do you suggest? In my opinion, that should be done in the examination-in-chief. But in any event we are where we are. What is your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honours, I have a question as to whether Your Honours will allow in-court identifications by the witness. And secondly, Your Honour, if that is true, we agree that typically that is done in direct examination. In this instance, we believe that it was better to wait for cross-examination to see if identities were actually put into question. We believe that it was done so, and that is why we now, with this witness, ask to be allowed to do it in cross-examination. So we really have, I guess, two questions: one pertaining only to this witness and the other a much broader one, which is, will you allow in-court identification by the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Can you cite us to any jurisprudence in the Tribunal that would say that we shouldn't? It's standard practice in some of our operating systems to have in-court identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: It's been allowed in other cases. It's typically been a topic of discussion so that the Judges indicate whether they allow it, because some jurisdictions do not allow in-dock identifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for the translation. There's always this question of translation. Has the Defence got a spokesman who could comment on this or is each one of you going to respond? So you're going to respond on behalf of all Defence counsel or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't think I can respond on behalf of the other counsel. I don't know what they're going to say at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, if you have not been authorised, then I have to consult the Defence counsel in the order. So I apologise, Mr. O'Sullivan. So let me consult Mr. Krstan Simic on this point. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we believe that this should have been done during the examination-in-chief. This was supposed to be raised by the Prosecutor in the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In my submission, in-dock identification should not be permitted. I recognise in some jurisdictions it is, but in those where it's not, there's good reason. I submit the reasons that it is not because of the facility with which a person in the dock can look over and determine who is who in the court, and the weight that Your Honours gain from such in-dock identification is minimal at best. It accomplishes very little. It is highly prejudicial to the accused and does very little to go to identification of events that may have happened in this case as many as eight years ago. So in my submission, it's an unreliable, highly prejudicial, unfair procedure for the witness to attempt to identify someone in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of the accused Radic does not dispute his identity. In our legal system, in-dock identifications are permitted, and I couldn't object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that this method has already been applied before this Tribunal, in particular in the Tadic case. However, in view of the overall circumstances, this type of evidence could not have any significant weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovan Simic. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] We do not object to this type of identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the request by the Prosecution, and in view of the submissions made by the Defence, the Chamber believes that as regards the interests of justice, there are some unfavourable conditions because this is a multi-defendant trial. There are, of course, other adverse circumstances as regards this type of identification. However, on the other hand, it is beyond dispute that these persons were present in Omarska. This is not contested. So the Chamber will authorise this type of identification to be made and will ask all the persons concerned to behave in a civilised way by doing so. So let me address the witness now. Could the witness put on his earphones. Oh, I'm sorry, Mr. O'Sullivan. Not yet, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have a further objection and that is the point as to whether or not this identification which you appear to be allowing can take place during redirect. My learned friend has said that during cross-examination, and I'm referring to the cross-examination by Kos, the issue of identity was raised. I submit it was not. I did not talk about whether or not this person recognised Kos. That was not at all the scope or the questions I put in cross-examination, and I submit it's inappropriate to attempt, at this point, to go beyond the scope of my cross-examination. My cross-examination did not deal or question the identity of Mr. Kos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan, we have reached a ruling. We have already made a decision. What is the meaning of your intervention now? I don't understand. We have closed the debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There are two questions. One which I've understand you to decide is that you will allow in-court identification. In my submission, that cannot take place in re-examination unless that issue was raised and left unclear during cross-examination. My cross-examination did not deal with the question of identification of Mr. Kos. Therefore, in my submission, this matter cannot be dealt with on re-examination. It wasn't even raised on cross and therefore can't be an unclear matter for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, can you clarify for us on what basis you think the identification question was raised in cross-examination, particularly with reference to the Kos cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, it is the Prosecution's submission that the cross-examination which dealt with whether or not Krle was mentioned in the 1994, 1995 statement was put in the record for the inference that Krle was not part of the -- that the person, this accused called Krle was not part of the incident with Brk. The Prosecution's view is that it calls into question who participated in that incident and that includes the identity of those individuals, one of them being named Krle. That's the position for Krle. Your Honour, I notice your reaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My immediate reaction is it's a bit of a stretch, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and certainly that would be a fair interpretation but that is our position. That is our interpretation of that question. As for Kvocka, the question was this person who you knew so well, you never talked about. Again, we believe the implication is that if he's talking about someone, it's not Kvocka, it's not the person he has testified here today. So we believe these raise the questions of about whom is he speaking and is he speaking about the person he now, in court, calls Kvocka. Those are the reasons we believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, my own reaction is -- and you've come away with certainly a good half a loaf by getting ruling in favour of in-court identification as a general matter, at least, in direct. I continue, at least, subject to conference with my colleagues, to be sceptical of whether or not the question of identification was really raised in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I certainly accept that Your Honour. We did indicate we believe there are two questions. That is the Prosecution's basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having heard this additional clarification, we have one additional reason too for the following: The witness has made reference to a number of nicknames during his testimony and from the point of -- from the interests of justice, it is also important for us to know who he was referring to. The Chamber will therefore allow in-court identification. Ms. Hollis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If the witness could put the headphones back on, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Beganovic, during your testimony, you have indicated that of the people you spoke about that are relevant here, you knew one person before the camp and that was Mr. Kvocka. Mr. Beganovic, are you able today to recognise Mr. Kvocka, and if you are able to do so, could you please point to him and identify him for the record.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes, he is sitting in the last row. He's the second of those civilians sitting there; second one from the left. He's sitting next to Krkan, and he's slightly balding. I don't know if this is enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: He's wearing a dark blazer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you just mentioned that he was sitting next to the person that you have referred to as Krkan. Will you please make that identification and tell the Judges where Krkan is sitting.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: He's the first one from the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you speaking of the left as I would be looking at the person?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes. From our -- I mean from my left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Beganovic, you also testified about a person you identified with the nickname of Krle. Are you able to recognise Krle today and, if so, would you please point to him and identify him.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes. He's sitting in the last row. He's the third one from the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also made mention of a person by the name of --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, shall I go through all of them or just the ones I thought were in question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Third one from the left starting to count from the left or -- please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes, if you start counting from the left. From my left side. He's the third one in line, civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Beganovic, you have now made a reference to a man you called Zigic?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes. He's sitting in the second row from the right. He's the first one from the right-hand side, the first civilian. He is wearing a dark blazer and a blue shirt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your right?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes, from the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned a Mr. Prcac and you said that before the camp, you had no personal knowledge of him. Are you able to recognise Prcac?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes. He is the second civilian from the left-hand side sitting in the second row.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which row are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: The second row. He's sitting next to Zigic. He's the second civilian sitting in the second row from the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Hollis. Judge Riad. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Beganovic.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just would like to understand some points more clearly from your long testimony, without entering into details. We will start at the beginning when you started testifying, and you were mentioning that the area of Stari Grad, which had something like 200 buildings, was set on fire and flattened by bulldozers. Did that happen during a fight? Was there some kind of insurrection of the town which led to this drastic measure?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: No. No, there was no fighting at all in the area of Stari Grad, and Stari Grad was intact until the 30th of May, around 12.00. In the afternoon of that day, a number of houses were set on fire, including my family house which was set on fire. This is at least what I assumed was going on on that day, as I was observing it from the window of Dr. Sadikovic's house. It turned out to be true later on, and it was my parents' house. Another house on the other side of the town was also destroyed, and the area was later on destroyed with a bulldozer. There are no more old houses in the area of Stari Grad. Only the two state-owned businesses remained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mean no specific events led to that? You were not expecting that? You were living in peace until that time?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: There were absolutely no reasons for arson and destruction, but this was the policy they followed. They wanted to force the population to move out, not only in the area of Stari Grad but in the municipality of Prijedor as a whole. They wanted to force the Muslim population, as well as the majority of the Croatian population, to move out of town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said this was the policy. Was it announced by the media? How did you know that it was a policy and not done just by some gangsters?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Well, they were all gangsters. All those who were wearing uniform, they all acted in the same way. They obeyed orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So they were wearing uniforms? Those who set the fire, they were wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were. Some were wearing police uniforms and some, military uniforms. Most of them were military uniforms. And quite a few of those who were wearing police uniforms did the same thing as those wearing military uniforms. The type of uniform was not really important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you know about it before? Did you expect it? Was it happening all around you and you were just waiting for your turn?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: You're referring to the 30th of May, or in general?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In general.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Well, this applied to all Muslims living in the area of the Prijedor municipality. However, the first victims were wealthier Muslims, intellectuals, doctors, and so on. That part of the population was the first victim. My house was set on fire on the 29th of May, in the evening hours, around 11.00, so a day before the alleged attack on Prijedor. And the fire department didn't even try to react and try to put out the fire. So my house on the Esada Midzica Street was set on fire on the 29th of May. And the restaurant that was located next to the house, they didn't touch that because it was a new building. I had just built it. And later on it was vandalised; they took everything that was of any value from that restaurant. And the area in question now is a parking lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: May I just mention that you said that you went to Dr. Esad Sadikovic's house and it was not burnt. Why this discrimination? He was also an eminent person, wasn't he? Why did they give him this special treatment? Did they have some people who were friends and some people who were enemies amongst the Muslims? Was there any discrimination?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: No, they probably didn't plan to set that part of the town or fire and to destroy it. But the area of Stari Grad bothered them because it was inhabited almost 100 per cent by Muslims and the land was privately owned by the inhabitants who lived there. So this fact probably bothered them. There had been attempts prior to that, during communism, to move us out. They wanted to construct some sports facilities. But most of the people stayed, they didn't want to move out. So this is why the area of Stari Grad fell within the scope of their plan, because all of the land was privately owned. The area of Stari Grad was privately owned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. But things did not stop at Stari Grad, it continued elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Things continued elsewhere and included the area of Zegar, then the area of Carakovo, Brdo, Hambarine, Biscani, Rizvanovici, Rakovcani, all of which are 100 per cent Muslim areas. This was all destroyed, including the town of Kozarac, which was a 98 per cent Muslim town. So wherever the population was majority Muslim, the area was destroyed, 90 per cent of the area was destroyed. And whatever remained was later used by Serbs from other parts of the country, from Knin, for example. There are Serbs living in Muslim houses now, and we are still unable to go back today, in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Speaking of going back, this is just a digression, you are still living in Holland, are you? You have a flower shop.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You are not thinking of going back.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: I am going back to Prijedor. This year I took part in municipal elections, I was listed as an independent candidate, and I will go back, regardless of the results of the elections. I wish to continue doing business in my hometown. I want to go back, I want to start anew, and this is the only objective in my life for the time being. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, there was an incident where you said they read you instructions where Muslims had to wear white ribbons and form a line and go out. First, these white ribbons, was it a rule to go around with white ribbons all the time, or was it just in this incident? Was there a rule that Muslims should go around in the street with a white ribbon?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: As far as I know they had to on that day. What happened later on, I don't know. I was in the camp. Nobody was allowed out in the street without a white ribbon because his life would be in danger because he would be accused of trying to pass himself for a Serb. That was the situation those days. Whoever would come out in the street would be wearing a white ribbon. This is what I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And when you wear a white ribbon, how are you treated?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't understand. What do you mean "treated"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: If you don't wear a white ribbon, you are killed. And if you wear a white ribbon, how are you treated?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: At that time we were branded as Muslims and we were sent to the camp, like what happened to the Jews during the Second World War. We were marked with that white ribbon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. Now, when you were wearing the white ribbon and you were walking to the centre of town, you saw piles of dead civilians; some of them were mutilated. Did you see that? Did you see them being mutilated, or you just thought they were mutilated? Did it happen before your eyes, the mutilation, the torture, in the street?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: No, not in the street. I passed by four or five bodies put on a pile, on top of one another, and in my opinion they looked as if they had been massacred by bursts of gunfire. They had injuries all over their bodies, so this must have been the result of bursts of gunfire. But I wasn't paying too much attention to that. I turned around and I saw other bodies on the market as well, but then I could no longer watch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you said that Mr. Kvocka --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Kvocka would come to the camp in a 190 Mercedes, distribute cigarettes, and walk around and issue orders. Could you more or less describe his position in the hierarchy of the camp? Was he obeyed by everyone? Was he respected by everyone?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes, he was obeyed; he was respected. He was a boss to them. He was a commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned that his mother-in-law was more or less an acquaintance of your mother. Was that right?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: They were friends. They had been friends for years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And then you mentioned that you found an order -- this man, I think, who wanted to kill you told you that there was an order by Kvocka that you should be killed. Was that right? Nikica.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was Nikica Janjic who told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He said, "Emir Beganovic, kop 2."

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes, that's what was written on the note. "Emir Beganovic, kop 2."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: If it was a friend of your mother's, why would he do that, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, there was no longer any friendship between Muslims and Serbs, except for some very isolated cases involving a Serb helping Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was Mr. Kvocka considered in the camp by the Muslims as a friend of the Muslims, having as his family-in-law Muslims?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: I didn't see that. But as far as I know, two of his brothers-in-law came to the camp but they didn't stay very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How were they treated, his brothers-in-law? Did they have any privileged treatment?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: I cannot speak about that, whether they did or didn't, because I was in a different room. I didn't see them at all in the camp. This is what I heard from other detainees, that they were there. But as far as I know, no, they were not physically mistreated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But only his brothers-in-law. The other Muslims did not benefit from this kindness.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Nobody had any nice treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said that you were without food for six days and without water, and you were taken and beaten and so on. Was there any way of presenting a demand or a complaint to the administration there?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: We didn't dare ask to go to the toilet, never mind to complain to someone. As soon as you complained, you could lose your life. It was not possible to complain. And if somebody saw that somebody had bruises, then he would hit him even more, "He's Alija's Mujahedin, so let's hit him harder, until he dies." People even concealed the fact that they were injured so that others wouldn't see that the previous one had beaten him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you feel at any moment that the people who beat you and mistreated you were separate from the administration, that the people at the top didn't know about it?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: No, not for a moment. They knew everything; I can guarantee that. All the detainees can confirm that, that those up there knew everything, those on top in the administration. In fact, it is the people in the administration who did most of the killings and the mutilations. Ninety-five per cent, I can say, came from those offices where we were interrogated, beaten up; maybe even a higher percentage. By chance I was among the few who was interrogated and was given water, and a cigarette was given to me. Drago Meakic interrogated me and Obrad Despot. Both of them used to work in the former SUP. Meakic even said that he knew that I was never involved in politics, that I was always in business, and he, for instance, treated me quite normally. I was surprised. I was half dead with fear when I entered there. But 95 of people came out beaten up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Beganovic, you testified that when people got to the centre of Prijedor, the men were put on buses and taken to Omarska, or at least the men of a normal age, and the women and children were put on buses. Do you know what happened to the buses that took the women and children? Were you in a position to know where they went or what was done with them?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: I don't know afterwards what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: The men --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You also testified that you were on the pista for, I think, it was over 10 days, 10 to 15 or 10 to 20 days, and your first day was May 30th, I think. So that would place you on the pista for most of the time, except when they took you in for the rain, between May 30th and mid-June; is that right? That was the period that you were out on the pista. I just want to nail that down.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You stated that you had formally been a member of the army, the JNA, so you have some familiarity with army discipline and hierarchy. During the period that you were in Omarska, did there appear to you to be a kind of police or military discipline in effect between the guards and their superiors and the administration? Did it appear to you that there was an army-like discipline, or were people just doing whatever they felt like, in terms of the guards and other officials? Did you see evidence of a regular army or police-like discipline or hierarchy in effect during the period that you were at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: There was nothing there, no discipline or hierarchy. It was lawlessness. People could do whatever they wanted. People could have killed as many people as they wanted without anybody asking why or how. Everyone came to settle their personal accounts there. If they had some verbal disputes, if people hated someone, they would come to Omarska and they would kill them. There were absolutely no rules. None at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me ask you the question slightly differently -- I have your answer to that question -- and that is, many times in your testimony you did refer to, I think, both Mr. Kvocka and, at a later point, Mr. Radic as being bosses, that they gave orders, which did suggest to me that there was some kind of hierarchy, people who gave orders to other people. Is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: No, you're not wrong. But they were orders to beat up people, mistreat people, rather than the other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. I understand your point. But my question was directed at the notion that there were some people, at least I read that from your testimony, among the guards who were in a superior position, who gave orders to other guards to do something, whether it was good or bad. Is that right? I mean, you referred to people as bosses and you referred to Mr. Kvocka, at one point, as a commander. So I'm asking you the basis for that. Did you actually see, or was it that you heard about certain people being the bosses of other people, being in a position to give other guards orders?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Yes, they were commanders. But we never saw any one of those commanders tell an ordinary guard, "Don't do that. Why are you mistreating the man?" and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that very well, and I have your point taken. But I am just trying to establish the basis on which you understood, for instance, Mr. Kvocka, to be a commander, which you referred to, or Mr. Radic to be a shift commander. Was it that you yourself saw them giving orders to other guards, or you were told by other people that they were commanders or shift commanders, or that they told you themselves they were? Just the basis on which you knew they were bosses.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: They simply -- when we were on the pista, we could see that they were giving orders to these ordinary guards, and then they also addressed them as commanders. And simply, they were commanders to these ordinary guards and they were addressed as such, and all the detainees knew that Krkan was shift leader, that Kvocka is Krkan's commander and the commander of the others. That was clear to every one of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You mentioned, just in answer to one of Judge Riad's questions, that Mr. Meakic, whom you knew previously, had been one of your interrogators and that he had behaved relatively decently toward you. That, I take it, was toward the end of your detention. Did you see Mr. Meakic around the camp in the first days of your detention while you were on the pista? Was he at the camp, to your knowledge? Do you remember seeing him in those early days?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: I cannot remember seeing him. But when I went in for interrogation, I saw him for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. But that was later on, I think, probably late -- according to your own testimony --

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: This must have been at the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I agree. Just a few more questions. Now, when you said that you would see Mr. Kvocka and Mr. Radic acting as bosses, giving some kind of orders to guards, would you see them acting as bosses only to the police officials or to the soldiers who were around in the camp too? In other words, were they acting as bosses over just people coming out of the police station in Omarska or to other members of the army who might be around the camp?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: The ordinary guards were treated in the same way as those who wore a blue uniform. There was no distinction between them. They acted in the same way; they could mistreat like the others. Of course Kvocka was in charge of all of them, as far as I know. But what was actually happening up there at the top, I really don't know who Kvocka was accountable to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Two more questions. One, you told us, I believe, that you saw Mr. Kvocka around the camp. I think you used the term at one point, "He was all over the camp." Was that in the early days only? Did you see him many times or only once or twice in July and August? Was he still around the camp, the way he had been in the early days, in July and August?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: In August I didn't see him. At the beginning of July I would still see him, until Mr. Prcac came to replace him. I don't know exactly but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: [Question obscured by translation]

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'll finish up here. You talked about hearing screams at night sometimes or moans of pain. Were those all men, or did you ever hear women's screams?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: I can't say that I heard women screaming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. My last question. After you left the camp and you spent months in the other two camps, Manjaca and Batkovic, were the conditions better there? Were the prisoners treated better there than in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: If I were to compare them, I would say that Manjaca was a camp and Omarska was hell. It can't even be called a camp; it was simply hell, every minute of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So the conditions were worse in Omarska than in the other two camps that you spent time in. My very last question, then, is: Were the other men that were with you in those other two camps later, Manjaca and Batkovic, were they also just civilians like you? They weren't people who had been captured by the Serbian army, were they? Or were they? Were they just people who had been picked up in the various towns, the way you had been?

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: One-hundred per cent civilian population. There wasn't a single one in uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: "Why didn't you mention this fact?"
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. I don't have any questions, Witness. Therefore, this brings to an end your testimony. Before you leave, we have to deal with the exhibits. I think we only have Exhibit D1/2. Mr. O'Sullivan has tendered it into evidence, Madam Hollis did not object, so it is admitted into evidence. I think there are no other questions to deal with. Mr. Dubuisson.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is quite so. But we must remember that there was an exhibit submitted by the Prosecutor, and also another one this morning, a plan, a detailed plan of the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was the point I was going to raise, that I believe those were offered and admitted, and that would have been 3/76 and 3/77. Your Honour, at the break I also spoke with the Defence about the references to the trial transcript of Mr. Beganovic in the Tadic case, and I believe the Defence would like to offer that into evidence. Perhaps I'm misspeaking for them, so I'll let them speak for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the exhibits that Madam Hollis would like to tender, I think that the Defence had no objections. Are there any objections of the Defence in relation to the admission of these exhibits? Thank you very much, Mr. O'Sullivan. Thank you. So they are admitted as well. Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence would also like to -- the Defence of Mr. Kvocka would like to tender into evidence Mr. Beganovic's statement, at the end of 1994, beginning of 1995, and the transcript of his testimony in the Tadic case. Those documents have already been marked, and I think there's no objection, but we would like them to be admitted as Defence exhibits. Also, in view of certain confusion about court rulings, during the testimony of an expert witness on police law, we will submit these documents regarding sentences. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the transcript of the Tadic case is a public document. No? So we need to tender it into evidence. If it was a public document -- Madam Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't shaking my head "no" at that. It was in open session; it is a public document. If Your Honours can simply take copies of it and if we don't have to tender those, that would be easier. It's certainly your decision on that. But it was offered in open session, so it would be a public document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the other hand, there is the same document that Mr. Simic used, it is the same document tendered by Mr. O'Sullivan. So perhaps I should like to ask the registrar. Mr. Dubuisson, we have a public document, the transcript, and we have already admitted 1/2. It is the same document which Mr. Simic wishes to tender. What is the practical solution, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The exhibit is D1/2, "2" indicating the number attached to the accused. It is clear that once an exhibit has been admitted, it is admitted into the file of the case. Regardless which Defence counsel tendered the exhibit, it becomes part of the case file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it can be used by all the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, regarding the Tadic transcript, what about that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clearly admitted by the Chamber that the transcript should be considered as an exhibit in this case, and it will be so. We will make a copy and a copy will be distributed of the Tadic testimony, and we will give it a number. If it's a document of the Prosecution, it will carry a Prosecution number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was used by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It can be "/1", saying that it is on behalf of Krstan Simic that it is being tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please will you mark this transcript. I think it is better to have all these documents in our file. Which is the number for Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be D24/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Tadic transcript. And for the witness statements?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That has already been admitted. That is D1/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we've dealt with all that. Are there any other remarks or observations? I think the exhibits have been dealt with now. Witness, thank you very much for coming here. We wish you to be able to resume the friendships that you had, to be able to forget hatred, and to be a good witness of peace and good relations with other people, those who have other political options, other religious, even, beliefs and ethnic beliefs. So thank you very much. You may go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis, before the break, and to prepare things in advance -- I see that Mr. Fila wishes to take the floor. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I want to raise a matter of principle in this case, if I may. When the Prosecutor examines, or we do, the other party has the right to object. Of course we don't have the right when one of you Honourable Judges are questioning the witness. But I wanted to make a request, if possible, because when Judge Wald was asking the witness, she said that the witness at one point said that Mladjo Radic was a shift commander and that he issued orders and that he was an important person in the camp. I claim that he never said that until the Judge put the question to him in that way. What is my ability to react in such situations if the witness is said to have said something that he didn't say. Nowhere in the transcript will you find that he said that Mladjo Radic was the shift commander, but after this was suggested to him, he confirmed that. If I am asking -- if somebody was something and what he was, I will probably be prevented from doing so, but that rule must apply to all of us. So we've now come to this fact that Mladjo Radic was shift commander and this is something that the witness did not say in response to my question. He never said that he was an important person, nor that he had important duties. So could this go down in the record as my remark and in future, if the witness is said to have told that he said something, then the exact page and line should be quoted. I have to protest in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, you know that we cannot hear you because we are all tired. The time has run out for regulating organisation. We have had the witness taken out and it is time for the next witness to come in. Mr. Simic, what is your question? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do have a question which is along the same lines as Mr. Fila's. We are placed in a position not to be able to clarify certain points. Her Honour, Judge Wald, was talking about Meakic, Drago Meakic. He has nothing in common with Zeljko Meakic, and we had no opportunity to clear up this question that it was an investigator and not a member of the security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you repeated what Mr. Simic has already said. Never mind though. What I am going to ask Madam Hollis, we're going to have a protected witness, I think; is that correct? It is. What protective measures have been asked for?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The protective measures are pseudonym, face distortion, and for part of the testimony, a private session. We would suggest that at the very beginning we would need a private session as we go through some personal matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So that is decided. Thank you for reminding me. I'm going to ask Mr. Dubuisson to prepare everything including having the witness in the courtroom, and we are going to have a half-hour break. As for the questions raised by the Defence, we're going to keep your remarks in mind and think them over. So now we are going to have a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Good afternoon, Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please read the solemn declaration that the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Thank you. Mr. Dubuisson will now show you a piece of paper which bears your name on it. You will simply indicate to us by saying yes or no if this is indeed your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. This is your name, but you will be referred to as Witness AJ. Am I right, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will first answer questions that will be put to you by Ms. Hollis. Ms. Hollis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution's understanding is that we are now in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have to state that we are in public session.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could we please go to private session for this time for background information about this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are in public session. You may continue, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AJ, I would now like to draw your attention to the 30th of May, 1992. On that date where were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I was staying with my neighbours some 50 metres away from my own house. And from there, when the attack of the 30th of May started, I crossed the River Berek Sana and went to a place called Ada and this is how I reached the house of my best man, Zijad Trnolic. I crossed the Berek creek and I reached his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could ask the witness to be able -- to be provided with Prosecution Exhibit 3/76, the map of Prijedor. If that could be placed on the ELMO, please. Can you pull it closer so that the witness can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you could take a moment to orient yourself on that map. You have referred to crossing the Berek. Can you take a look at that map and point for the Judges to what you mean by Berek, if you could point to the map on the overhead?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Berek, it's here [indicates]. It is a tributary to the Sana River which joins the Sana River again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you point again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So which looks to be a canal that joins off the Sana river is the Berek?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you indicated that you went to a house of your friend, again, pointing to the map, could you show the general area of the city that you went to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: This area here [indicates]. This is where we went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness AJ, after you arrived, when you arrived at this house, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: In that house, I saw about 100 people, women and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Half an hour, maybe one hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Then a woman came together with two or three soldiers in uniform who wore red berets and they told us to go out, to leave the house, all of us. So we went out and we went as far as the road. And this is where the men were lined up and they separated women and children from the men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you went to the road and you were separated, what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: They asked who had any weapons. I was afraid and I said I had a rifle and a pistol at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then after you told them you had the rifle and the pistol, then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Then they told me that I should go and fetch the weapons. So I went because it was in the vicinity between 50 and 100 metres away from there. And when I reached the back of the house, I saw a column of smoke and I thought that my house was on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: People from the town, the citizens that were walking on the other side, including women and children -- they were walking in a column -- they were escorted by the police, by reservists. So I joined that column.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you joined that column, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: To the Balkan Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you went along with this group of people, did you recognise any of the uniformed personnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you recognise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Bato Kovacevic. Cvijic; I don't know his first name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people that you recognised, what was their ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you arrived at the Hotel Balkan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: There were many of us there; the hotel was full. There were women, children, men. And some time later, buses arrived and they drove people away. I don't know where to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were there at the Hotel Balkan, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I went to the reception because I wanted to call a friend of mine, Slobodan Balaban, who was a specialist, a doctor. When I called him from the reception, he was at home and he asked me where I was. I told him I was at the hotel and he said, "I'll be right there in a minute."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: In the meantime, Ranko Vujasinovic came. He touched me on my shoulder and he asked me what I was doing there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I told him I was waiting for Batan, whom he also knew; he probably knew him better than I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Then he cursed my mother, he kicked me in my buttocks, and he took a bayonet, but Ritan, who was the chief of the reception, was there. Ranko Stojanovic was also there. And they sort of told me, "What are you doing? Are you normal?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
